tldr: In bilateral teleoperation of nonlinear, multi-DOF robots under constant communication delays, this paper achieves both delay-independent stability and high force transparency by directly reflecting environmental contact forces to the master, using LMI-based quantification of passivity shortage combined with an upper strictly passive communication law.
hero_caption: The velocity-force nonlinear teleoperation architecture targeted by the proposed method. Environmental contact force $F_e$ is directly fed back to the master side over the communication channel, while the passivity shortage on the remote side is offset and stabilized by the channel's own upper strict passivity.
overview:
In bilateral teleoperation, where a robot is controlled remotely, communication delays have long been known to destabilize the closed-loop system. To address this, passivity-based approaches such as wave transformation (WT) have been widely used. However, to preserve stability, most conventional methods transmit a virtual coordinating force rather than the direct contact force. This introduces a tradeoff that degrades the fidelity (transparency) of haptic feedback felt by the operator.

Recently, methods have been proposed to compensate for the passivity shortage on the remote side—caused by directly sending back contact forces—using an intentionally over-dissipative channel, known as an upper strictly passive (USP) communication law. However, these methods were restricted to 1-DOF linear robots. Real robots are nonlinear, multi-DOF systems with Coriolis forces, centrifugal forces, and configuration-dependent inertia, so those earlier results cannot be applied directly.

This work extends that approach to general multi-DOF nonlinear Euler–Lagrange robots. First, the authors derive a method to quantitatively evaluate the passivity shortage of the remote side by solving linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). Next, they design a vectorized USP wave-transformation communication law tailored to cancel this shortage. Using a Lyapunov–Krasovskii approach, they mathematically prove that the system is stable regardless of the delay duration, while also achieving position tracking during free motion and force tracking during hard contact.

Numerical simulations using a 2-DOF nonlinear planar manipulator (with a one-way delay of 0.2 s in a hard wall contact scenario) show that optimizing the communication parameters delivers smooth, non-divergent position tracking under delay, as well as high force fidelity with an RMS force tracking error of just 1.2993 N.
contributions: Derived a framework to quantitatively evaluate the passivity shortage of a nonlinear multi-DOF remote robot with direct contact force feedback using linear matrix inequalities (LMIs)

Extended the upper strictly passive (USP) communication law, previously limited to 1-DOF linear models, to vectorized multi-DOF systems and proved delay-independent closed-loop stability using a Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional
Explicitly formulated theoretical conditions under which position synchronization during free motion and force synchronization during hard contact are asymptotically achieved
Proposed an offline optimization procedure for communication parameters to minimize force and position tracking errors while satisfying stability bounds

sections.heading: Direct Contact Force Feedback: Overcoming Delays and Nonlinearity
sections.summary: In teleoperation over communication delays, balancing stability and haptic transparency has long been a challenge. Because existing direct force feedback methods using over-passive channels were limited to 1-DOF linear systems, this paper aims to extend the idea to multi-DOF nonlinear robots.
sections.details:
In master-slave bilateral teleoperation, an operator's motions are transmitted to a remote robot, and the reaction forces from the remote environment are reflected back to the operator to provide an immersive operational feel. However, when delays are introduced into the communication channel, the control loop can generate energy, causing the entire closed-loop system to oscillate violently and become unstable.

To prevent delay-induced instability, wave transformation (WT) and scattering transformation based on passivity theory have been widely used. However, feeding direct environmental contact forces into a conventional passive communication channel renders the remote side (robot + controller + environment) non-passive (energy-generating), causing the system to fail. Because of this, mainstream designs have transmitted a coordinating force computed from position errors rather than the direct contact force. Unfortunately, this fails to accurately convey environmental stiffness and subtle contact sensations to the operator, severely degrading teleoperation transparency.

To tackle this challenge, recent work (Tho and Miyoshi, 2023) introduced the upper strictly passive (USP) communication law. This law deliberately builds excess energy dissipation (upper strict passivity) into the channel to cancel the passivity shortage on the remote side. However, this breakthrough and subsequent developments remained confined to 1-DOF linear robot models. Real articulated robots are nonlinear, multi-DOF systems subject to dynamic coupling and configuration-dependent inertia variations, so the theory could not be applied as-is. In this paper, the authors set out to quantify the passivity shortage for nonlinear multi-DOF Euler–Lagrange systems and construct a multi-DOF-ready USP communication law.

sections.heading: System Formulation: Modeling Nonlinear Robots with Direct Force Reflection
sections.summary: The master and remote robots are modeled using multi-DOF nonlinear Euler–Lagrange equations under constant communication delays. To boost transparency, environmental contact force is fed back directly, and the core strategy is to suppress the resulting instability through the communication channel.
sections.details:
The teleoperation system considered in this study consists of a local (master) robot operated by a human and a remote (slave) robot interacting with the work environment. Both robots are described by general nonlinear Euler–Lagrange equations with inertia matrix $M_i(q_i)$, Coriolis and centrifugal matrix $C_i(q_i, \dot{q}_i)$, and gravity term $G_i(q_i)$ for $i \in \{m, s\}$.

The human hand force $F_h$ is modeled with hand spring stiffness $K_h$ and an exogenous muscle force $f_h^\star$. The environmental contact force $F_e$ is expressed as the product of the environment's stiffness matrix $K_e(q_s, \dot{q}_s)$ and the remote position $q_s$. Each robot is regulated by a local controller featuring gravity compensation and damping injection. The critical design choice here is that the environmental contact force $F_e$ measured at the remote side is sent directly to the master through the communication channel, rather than as a virtual coordinating force.

With this direct contact force feedback, the input-output mapping from velocity command $\dot{q}_{sd}$ to contact force $F_e$ in the remote closed-loop dynamics loses passivity, exhibiting energy-generating behavior. The goal of this research is to compensate for this passivity shortage using the upper strict passivity of the communication channel. This ensures overall closed-loop stability despite a round-trip delay $T$, while achieving high-precision position tracking in free motion ($q_s \to q_m$) and force tracking during contact ($F_h \to F_e$).

To make the analysis tractable, the authors introduce Assumption 1: remote position $q_s$ and velocity $\dot{q}_s$ remain inside a bounded compact set. This assumption is physically natural given practical workspace limits and damping injection. Since the subsequent stability analysis proves global boundedness for the whole system, the logic avoids circularity.

captions.P2: Overall block diagram of the velocity-input, force-feedback teleoperation system considered in this paper. Master velocity $\dot{q}_m$ and remote contact force $F_e$ are exchanged over the communication channel, balancing mutual energy exchange across the delay.

sections.heading: Measuring Passivity Shortage: Quantitative Evaluation via LMIs
sections.summary: A theorem is presented to quantify how much passivity is lost when contact forces are reflected directly back from the remote system. By organizing the nonlinear dynamics through an augmented state space, the problem is recast as solving linear matrix inequalities (LMIs).
sections.details:
To successfully stabilize the system, one must precisely know how much passivity the remote closed-loop system loses under direct force feedback. Without this exact number, it is impossible to determine how much energy the communication channel needs to dissipate.

The authors define an augmented state vector $x := (\dot{q}_s, q_s, q_{sd}) \in \mathbb{R}^{3n}$ and introduce a quadratic storage function $V_s(x) = x^\top P x$, where $P$ is a symmetric positive-definite matrix. They then derive a dissipation inequality for the input-output pair $(F_e, \dot{q}_{sd})$ in Theorem 1. Specifically, they establish conditions under which the time derivative $\dot{V}_s(x)$ satisfies:
$$\dot{V}_s(x) \le F_e^\top \dot{q}_{sd} + \alpha \dot{q}_{sd}^\top \dot{q}_{sd} - \lambda \dot{q}_s^\top \dot{q}_s$$
Here, $\alpha > 0$ represents the passivity shortage parameter, and $\lambda > 0$ represents the excess velocity dissipation.

This condition is formulated as a state-dependent linear matrix inequality (LMI):
$$A_2(p, v)^\top P A_1 + A_1^\top P A_2(p, v) + A_3(p, v) \preceq 0$$
If a constant matrix $P$ and scalars $\alpha, \lambda$ can be found such that this LMI holds across the entire remote operational range ($p \in \mathcal{P}, v \in \mathcal{V}$), the remote system is guaranteed to lack passivity by at most $\alpha$. In practical computation, $\alpha$ can be evaluated numerically using a grid-based method or polytopic techniques across the state space.

sections.heading: Multi-DOF USP Communication: Neutralizing Shortage for Guaranteed Stability Under Delay
sections.summary: To cancel the computed passivity shortage $\alpha$, a multi-DOF vectorized USP communication law with excess passivity is formulated. A Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional proves delay-independent stability and signal boundedness, while revealing conditions for position tracking in free motion and force tracking during contact.
sections.details:
This section presents the core of the method across four steps: communication law formulation, stability proof, transparency analysis, and parameter optimization.

- Communication Law Structure:
The classical wave transformation is extended to multi-DOF vectors, introducing a characteristic impedance $b > 0$ and upper strict passivity parameters $\gamma_l \le 0$ (master side) and $\gamma_r \le 0$ (remote side). Eliminating wave variables $u_m, v_m, u_s, v_s$ in favor of physical variables ($\dot{q}_m, F_e, \dot{q}_{sd}, F_{md}$) reveals that the remote velocity command $\dot{q}_{sd}$ obeys a delayed linear recurrence: $\dot{q}_{sd}(t) = \delta \dot{q}_{sd}(t - 2T) + \Delta(t)$. When $\gamma_r < 0$, the coefficient satisfies $|\delta| < 1$, making this recurrence exponentially stable on its own.

- Closed-Loop Stability Proof (Theorem 2):
A Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional $V$ is constructed by combining the kinetic energy of the robots, the human spring energy, the remote storage function $V_s$, and the energy stored in the communication channel $V_c = \int_{t-T}^t (|u_m|^2 + |u_s|^2) ds$. Taking its time derivative shows that the over-passivity term $\gamma_r |\dot{q}_{sd}|^2$ contributed by the channel directly adds to the remote passivity shortage term $\alpha |\dot{q}_{sd}|^2$ from Theorem 1. Therefore, selecting the communication parameter such that $\gamma_r < -\alpha$ (with $\gamma_l \le 0$) completely neutralizes the passivity shortage, leaving only negative dissipative terms: $\dot{V} \le -\frac{\beta_m}{2}|\dot{q}_m|^2 - \eta |\dot{q}_{sd}|^2 - \lambda |\dot{q}_s|^2$. This mathematically establishes boundedness of all signals and convergence of velocities to zero ($\dot{q}_m \to 0, \dot{q}_s \to 0$) regardless of the delay duration $T$.

- Transparency Analysis (Theorem 3):
In free motion ($F_e = 0$), if the impedance matching condition $\gamma_r = -1/(4b^2)$ holds, the position tracking error $e_q(t) = q_s(t) - q_m(t-T)$ asymptotically approaches zero up to an initial condition offset. During hard contact with a rigid wall, if master acceleration converges to zero in steady state, the operator force $F_h$ asymptotically matches the delayed contact force $F_e(t-T)$.

- Communication Parameter Optimization:
Subject to stability constraints ($0 < b < 1/(2\sqrt{\alpha})$ and $\gamma_l \le 0$), parameters are chosen to minimize a weighted integral-squared-error cost $J(b, \gamma_l)$ combining position and force tracking errors. Because simulation-based objective functions are often non-convex and non-smooth, the optimal parameter set is found offline using derivative-free optimization (patternsearch).

sections.heading: Validation on a 2-DOF Manipulator: Confirming Stability and High-Fidelity Force Transmission
sections.summary: Simulations using a 2-DOF planar manipulator under a 0.2 s one-way delay demonstrate the approach. With passivity shortage computed via LMIs and optimized communication parameters, the system achieves stable and accurate force reflection across alternating phases of free motion and wall contact.
sections.details:
To validate the theory, numerical simulations were carried out using identical 2-DOF planar manipulators (Euler–Lagrange systems with nonlinear inertia and Coriolis matrices) for both master and remote robots.

Simulation parameters were set as follows: human hand stiffness $K_h = 20I_2$ N/m, viscous damping $B_m = B_{s1} = 0.5I_2$ Ns/m, coordination gain $K_s = 100I_2$, and a one-way communication delay of $T = 0.2$ s (round-trip 0.4 s). On the remote side, a wall with stiffness $K_e = 100I_2$ N/m was placed at position $q_s = 0$, modeled with unilateral contact generating reaction forces only when penetrating into the negative region. The human target position $q_{md}$ was stepped between $\pm 0.1$ m with a 60-second period, reproducing alternating phases of free motion and hard wall contact.

First, across the operational space $\mathcal{P} \times \mathcal{V} = [-\pi, \pi]^2 \times [-1, 1]^2$ with a grid step of 0.1, the LMI condition (Theorem 1) was solved using YALMIP. With $\lambda = 0.001$, the passivity shortage was computed as $\alpha = 5.7709$. Over the stability region $0 < b < 0.208$ dictated by this $\alpha$, pattern search optimization prioritizing force tracking ($w_q = 0, w_f = 1$) yielded optimal parameters $b = 0.06$ and $\gamma_l = -20$ (resulting in $\gamma_r = -69.4444$).

In simulation, position trajectories remained fully stable without divergence. During wall contact, the remote arm cannot penetrate as deeply as the master command due to wall stiffness, leaving a steady-state position offset—which is physically expected under force control. In terms of force reflection, as seen in Fig. 4, the reflected force $F_h$ swiftly converged to the environment force $F_e$ following a brief transient upon contact. The overall RMS force tracking error remained remarkably low at 1.2993 N across the entire run.

captions.P8: Time history of environmental contact force $F_e$ and operator force $F_h$ (left) alongside force tracking error (right). Right after contacting the wall around 33 s, the error rapidly converges toward zero following a transient peak, demonstrating high force fidelity.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: This work establishes a framework for bilateral teleoperation of nonlinear multi-DOF robots with direct contact force feedback. Combining LMI-based quantification of passivity shortage with upper strictly passive communication achieves delay-independent stability alongside high haptic transparency.
sections.details:
This study establishes a bilateral teleoperation framework for nonlinear multi-DOF robots that directly feeds back environmental contact forces under constant communication delays. Its key achievement is that the passivity shortage arising from remote nonlinear dynamics is rigorously evaluated using LMIs and then canceled by a vectorized USP wave-transformation communication law, ensuring stability regardless of delay duration. Furthermore, simulation results demonstrate that communication parameter optimization allows both position tracking in free motion and highly accurate force reflection during contact.

For future work, the authors outline several research directions: accommodating dimension mismatch where master and slave have differing degrees of freedom or kinematic structures, extending to neural-network-inspired communication architectures to transmit richer information (such as velocity profiles), and conducting experimental validation on hardware platforms.

takeaways: Provides a clear design blueprint for the long-standing hurdle that direct force feedback causes instability, by quantifying remote passivity shortage via LMIs and canceling it with channel over-passivity.
Delivers a complete delay-independent stability proof (no divergence regardless of delay size) using a Lyapunov–Krasovskii functional while fully preserving Euler–Lagrange nonlinearities.
Employs a practical engineering approach that uses theoretical passivity bounds as search space constraints in offline optimization to maximize haptic transparency.
limitations: Relies on the assumption that remote position and velocity remain within a compact set (Assumption 1), providing local or semi-global rather than fully global guarantees.
Grid sampling the state space to solve the LMIs can suffer from the curse of dimensionality when scaling to systems with three or more degrees of freedom.
Assumes a constant communication delay, leaving direct handling of time-varying delays and packet loss typical of the internet as an open topic for future study.
